samples.summary: `--dry-run` is silently ignored by `api-keys create` / `revoke` / `list`, so the documented "preview a write first" safety control mints or destroys a real credential
samples.evidence:
This PR sweeps `--dry-run` across the remaining read commands and, at docs/design/cli.md:824-827, now states the contract unconditionally: "A dry run never reaches the network, so it burns no rate limit and emits no access log." The credential-management commands are the one namespace that was never swept. `registerApiKeysCommand` never reads `opts.dryRun`: api-keys.ts:15-17 goes straight to `getClient(opts).createApiKey(name)`, :43-45 to `revokeApiKey(keyId)`, :29-31 to `listApiKeys()`. Commander accepts the global `--dry-run` on every subcommand (root.ts:75), so the flag parses and is discarded.

Attack/failure chain: the CLI is explicitly aimed at agents, and the agent guidance says to preview writes with the flag — packages/cli/skills/SKILL.md:67 ("For write operations, run with `--dry-run` first to show intent"), docs/design/cli.md:905 ("`write` … Agent should confirm or use `--dry-run` first") and :1027. `wafflebase api-keys create ci-key --dry-run` therefore issues a live POST that mints a workspace-scoped API key and prints its secret (`schema/registry.ts:579` declares the response as `{ id, name, prefix, key }`) to stdout — into whatever agent transcript/CI log the user believed was showing an inert preview, with no revocation ever performed. `wafflebase api-keys revoke <id> --dry-run` (registry.ts:593 marks it `destructive`) irreversibly revokes the key the user was only asking to preview, breaking every consumer of that key. Both are credential-lifecycle side effects taken under a flag whose whole contract is "no side effect".

Every other write/destructive path in the CLI honours the flag (cells.ts:62/95/143, tabs.ts:47/71, docs.ts:108/143/161, files.ts:118/136, docs|notes|slides import), which is what makes the gap read as covered.

samples.summary: New §8.2 sentence states an unqualified "A dry run never reaches the network" that four commands still violate, turning a per-command note into a false global safety guarantee
samples.evidence: The sentence added at docs/design/cli.md:825-827 is scoped to reads in its first clause but its second clause is unconditional ("A dry run never reaches the network … even when the command is harmless"). Commands that still fetch under `--dry-run`: `api-keys create|list|revoke` (packages/cli/src/commands/api-keys.ts:17,31,45), `sheets export` (commands/sheets-export.ts:39 calls `getCells` unconditionally and then writes a local file), and `files get` (commands/files.ts:105). Because §8.4/§8.7 and the bundled skills tell agents to rely on this flag before writes, a design doc asserting the property globally is what makes an agent skip its own confirmation step for the commands where the property does not hold. Either scope the sentence to the enumerated commands or close the gaps.

samples.summary: Document/tab/cell identifiers are interpolated into request paths unencoded, so a crafted identifier redirects the authenticated request to an arbitrary path on the configured server (mirrored verbatim by the new dry-run preview)
samples.evidence: `getCell` (http-client.ts:345), `getCells` (:342), `setCell` (:348), `deleteCell` (:354), `listTabs` (:330) and `getDocument` (:199) build `/documents/${docId}/tabs/${tabId}/cells/${sref}` with raw template interpolation, unlike `downloadFileDocument` (:254) which does use `encodeURIComponent`. `wafflebase sheets cells get doc-1 '../../../../../auth/whoami'` produces a path that `fetch` normalises out of the workspace prefix, and the request still carries the `Authorization: Bearer` header assembled at :62-66 — i.e. an identifier from an untrusted source (an agent substituting a value from a document listing, a script reading ids from a shared file) can aim the user's credential at any GET/PUT/DELETE path on the configured host, relying on server-side authorisation alone to stop it. The new dry-run branch in commands/cells.ts:24-29 reproduces the same unencoded interpolation, so the preview faithfully mirrors — rather than reveals — the traversal. I could not demonstrate a privilege gain beyond what the caller's own token already permits, hence medium confidence on impact; the traversal itself is directly reachable.

verdict.reason: Verified independently: registerApiKeysCommand never reads opts.dryRun — create/list/revoke call getClient(opts).createApiKey/listApiKeys/revokeApiKey directly (api-keys.ts:17,31,45) and the file does not import printDryRun. I searched for an indirect guard and found none: HttpClient takes only CliConfig (http-client.ts:54) and its api-key methods fetch unconditionally (http-client.ts:365-389); getClient (root.ts:38-40) never forwards dryRun; buildProgram (cli.ts:17-33) installs no pre-action hook. A repo-wide grep for printDryRun|opts.dryRun shows every other write/destructive path guarded (docs.ts:108/143/161, tabs.ts:47/71, cells.ts:62/95/143, files.ts:118/136, notes.ts:89/107, slides.ts:94/112) with zero hits in api-keys.ts. The global --dry-run is declared at root.ts:75 so it parses on these subcommands and is discarded. The contract is stated unconditionally at docs/design/cli.md:809-810 and :824-827, and agents are told to preview writes with it (cli.md:905, :1027; skills/SKILL.md). Impact is security-relevant, not merely cosmetic: `api-keys create <name> --dry-run` mints a live credential and prints its secret (registry.ts:579 response includes `key`) into a transcript/CI log the caller believed was an inert preview, with no revocation; `api-keys revoke <id> --dry-run` irreversibly revokes (registry.ts:593 `destructive`). Major severity, credential-lifecycle side effects under a flag whose contract is "no side effect".

finding.summary: Document/tab/cell identifiers are interpolated into request paths without encodeURIComponent, so a caller-supplied id can retarget the credentialed request outside the workspace scope (path traversal / request-target injection)
finding.evidence: `getDocument(id)` builds `GET ${base}/documents/${id}` with no encoding (http-client.ts:199); same pattern at :330 listTabs, :340/:342 getCells (docId/tabId raw, only `range` encoded), :345 getCell, :348 setCell, :354 deleteCell, :361 batchCells. `base` is `${server}/api/v1/workspaces/${workspace}` (:82-85). `fetch` parses the string with the WHATWG URL parser, which collapses dot segments, so `docId = "../../../../workspaces/victim-ws/api-keys"` turns `wafflebase docs get <id>` into `GET ${server}/workspaces/victim-ws/api-keys` with the user's `Authorization: Bearer ...` header attached — i.e. the client-side workspace scoping in the path is bypassable and any endpoint on the configured host can be reached with the caller's credentials (only server-side authz stands between). The boundary is real because the CLI is explicitly built to be driven by agents (docs/design/cli.md:22-26, 1024-1029), which routinely pass document ids taken from untrusted content; the CLI then acts as a confused deputy. `downloadFileDocument` already uses `encodeURIComponent(docId)` (:254), showing the intended convention the other builders skip. The change under review propagates the same unencoded interpolation into new code (cells.ts:24, docs.ts:126, tabs.ts:15). Confidence is medium because exploitability depends on the backend's own authorization on the reached endpoint and on ids coming from an untrusted source.

verdict.reason: The finding is accurate as described. `base` is built at http-client.ts:82-85 as `${server}/api/v1/workspaces/${workspace}`, and identifiers are interpolated unencoded at http-client.ts:199 (getDocument), :202, :205, :283/:289 (doc content), :300/:306 (slides), :317/:323 (notes), :330/:333/:336 (tabs), and :342/:345/:348/:354/:361 (cells) — only `range` is encoded (:341). Every one of these goes through `request()` -> `send()` (:137), which attaches the `Authorization: Bearer` header from `authHeaders` (:59-69). `downloadFileDocument` at :254 uses `encodeURIComponent(docId)`, confirming the intended convention the other builders skip. No guard exists upstream: `getClient`/`getConfig` in commands/root.ts:24-40 pass commander args through untouched, and the command handlers (docs.ts:123-130, tabs.ts:12-19 and :63-78, cells.ts:16-39, :52-79, :91-105, :118-156) forward raw `<doc-id>`/`<tab-id>`/`<ref>` values; a repo-wide grep for `encodeURIComponent|validate` in packages/cli/src turns up no identifier validation anywhere. Because `fetch` normalises dot segments via the WHATWG URL parser, a caller-supplied id containing `../` retargets the credentialed request off the workspace-scoped prefix (e.g. to `${server}/workspaces/<ws>/api-keys`, an endpoint the same client reaches at :367). That is path traversal / request-target injection with the user's credentials attached — explicitly in the security lane. Impact is bounded by the backend's own authorization, which is why major rather than critical, but none of the three refutation grounds hold: the code is present as quoted, it is reachable and unguarded, and it is not out of lane.
